passage:
"Maria Didi, where are you putting Nani's glasses?"
"On the shelf, Akash. They'll get broken on the chair."
"But Nani went to the market. She saw them on the chair."
"Yes. So when she comes back, where will she look?"
"On the chair!" Akash laughed. "But they're not there!"
"Why will she look there?"
"Because she didn't see you move them. She thinks they're still on the chair."
"Good thinking. Let's tell her when she's home."

qa.q: Where did Maria put Nani's glasses?
qa.a: She put them on the shelf so they would not get broken on the chair.

qa.q: How does Akash feel about working out where Nani will look?
qa.a: Akash is amused, laughing because Nani didn't see Maria move the glasses and still believes they are on the chair.

qa.q: What did Maria do that helped Akash understand?
qa.a: She asked questions like "Where will she look?" and let Akash explain the reason without help.

qa.q: How might Nani feel if nobody told her about the move?
qa.a: She might be puzzled and worried when she finds the chair empty, so telling her saves her a scare.

grounding: A child works out that his grandmother still believes her glasses are where she left them.

passage: Observation note, Class KG-B. During puppet time I put a ball in the blue box while Bunny puppet watched, then sent Bunny away. Teddy moved the ball to the red box. I asked, "Where will Bunny look?" Hafsa jumped up: "Blue box! Bunny didn't see Teddy." Two classmates said red. Hafsa explained, "But Bunny wasn't here!" 👏 Tomorrow I'll let Hafsa run the puppets so others can guess and explain their answers. — Saurabh Sir

qa.q: Which box did Teddy move the ball to?
qa.a: Teddy moved the ball to the red box.

qa.q: How can you tell Hafsa felt confident about the answer?
qa.a: Hafsa jumped up to answer and kept explaining, "But Bunny wasn't here!" even when two classmates said red.

qa.q: How could the teacher support the classmates who said red?
qa.a: Letting Hafsa run the puppets and asking children to explain their guesses gives them another turn to notice who saw what.

qa.q: How might the two classmates see Hafsa's answer at first?
qa.a: They might think Hafsa is wrong, because they know the ball is in the red box and have not yet thought about what Bunny saw.

grounding: A teacher notes a child predicting that a puppet will act on an out-of-date belief.

passage: In the afternoon heat, Reena's goat wandered from the shed to the shade by the well. Reena watched her lie down. Soon Harish Bhaiya came up the lane with his school bag. "I'll give Chhoti her water in the shed," he said, picking up the bucket. Reena covered her mouth and giggled. "Bhaiya thinks she's in the shed!" she told Amma. "He didn't see her go." Then she ran after him. "Bhaiya, she's by the well!"

qa.q: Where did the goat go to lie down?
qa.a: She wandered from the shed to the shade by the well.

qa.q: Why did Reena giggle when Harish picked up the bucket?
qa.a: She was amused that he believed the goat was in the shed when she knew it wasn't.

qa.q: What choice did Reena make that was kind?
qa.a: After enjoying the joke, she ran after him to tell him the truth so he would not carry the bucket to an empty shed.

qa.q: How might Harish feel when he hears where Chhoti is?
qa.a: He would probably be relieved to save a trip and maybe amused that his little sister knew more than him this time.

grounding: A small-town girl realises her brother holds a mistaken belief about where the goat is.

passage: In a Johannesburg kitchen, Zanele watched Jin put his orange in the blue lunchbox and go out to wash his hands. Zanele's gogo, smiling, moved the orange into the fridge. 'When Jin comes back,' Gogo asked, 'where will he look?' Zanele giggled. 'In the blue box!' 'But the orange is in the fridge.' 'Yes, but Jin didn't see. He thinks it's still there.' She ran to meet him at the door.

qa.q: Where did Jin first put his orange?
qa.a: He put it in the blue lunchbox.

qa.q: Why did Zanele say Jin would look in the blue box?
qa.a: She understood that Jin did not see the orange being moved, so he would still believe it was in the box.

qa.q: How could Gogo keep this little game kind to Jin?
qa.a: She could make sure Jin gets his orange quickly and let the children laugh about the trick together, so no one feels fooled.

qa.q: What might Jin feel when he opens an empty lunchbox?
qa.a: He might feel surprised or confused for a moment, since his belief about the orange was wrong.

grounding: Illustrates a child understanding that someone else can hold a mistaken belief, set in South Africa.

passage: At the school activity room, Ganga Ma'am shook a crayon box. It rattled. 'What's inside, Hafsa?' 'Crayons!' Ma'am opened it. Pebbles! Hafsa laughed. 'Now,' said Ma'am, 'Didi from the next class is coming. What will she think is inside?' Hafsa bit her lip. 'Pebbles?' She paused and looked at the box again. 'No, wait. Crayons! She'll think crayons, because it's a crayon box. Only we know.'

qa.q: What was really inside the crayon box?
qa.a: Pebbles were inside the crayon box.

qa.q: How can you tell Hafsa was thinking hard before changing her answer?
qa.a: She bit her lip, paused and looked at the box again, seeming unsure, before realising that Didi would believe it held crayons.

qa.q: What could Ganga Ma'am ask next to deepen Hafsa's thinking?
qa.a: She could ask why Didi would think crayons, so Hafsa explains in her own words that Didi has not seen inside.

qa.q: How might Didi from the next class react when she sees the pebbles?
qa.a: She would likely be surprised, just as Hafsa was at first, because her belief would be wrong too.

grounding: Shows a child realising another person will hold a false belief based on what they have seen.
